title: Academy
lede: Four short lessons on how campaigning for young people actually works. Open one, read the steps and answer its question. Your progress is kept on this device only and nothing is sent anywhere.
rule: Facts in a lesson carry their source. Steps marked Editorial are this portal's own advice, built on the screens they link to.

sources.label: UK Parliament Petitions: how petitions work
UK Parliament: how MPs raise issues

modules.t: How a petition actually becomes a debate
modules.d: Thresholds, the Petitions Committee, and what a government response is and is not.

steps.t: It is open for six months
steps.d: A UK Parliament petition collects signatures for six months, then closes. Petition 754954 ran from 11 February to 11 August 2026.
At 10,000 signatures the Government must reply in writing.
At 100,000 the Petitions Committee considers it for a debate, which usually happens in Westminster Hall rather than the main Chamber.
In 2015 to 2017 only 4.5% of accepted petitions reached 10,000 signatures and 0.6% reached 100,000. Petition 754954 closed on 1,192.

steps.t: A response is not a change
steps.d: A written response states the Government's position. A debate means MPs discuss it. Neither changes the law on its own, so plan what you will do with the answer.

q.t: What does a petition get when it reaches 100,000 signatures?
opts: An automatic vote by all MPs
A meeting with the Prime Minister
q.why: At 100,000 signatures the Petitions Committee considers the petition for a debate. Nothing in the process changes the law automatically.

modules.d: Naming who is affected, asking for one clear thing, and where emotive tips into extreme.

steps.d: Say exactly what you want the Government or Parliament to do. A petition has to ask for something they can act on, so check the standards before you write.

steps.t: Name who is affected, with a real number
steps.d: Say who the change is for and how many people that is, using a figure you can source. The Young people in numbers screen has official figures to start from.

steps.t: Make it about the reader too
steps.d: People sign when they can see why it matters to someone they know. Give the reader a reason to care in one sentence.
Strong feeling helps; exaggeration, blame and claims you cannot back up lose trust and may break the rules. The Toolkit has wording you can adapt.

q.t: Which opening line asks for one clear action?
opts: Politics is broken and nobody cares about us
Fund free, non-partisan citizenship lessons in every secondary school
Young people deserve so much better
q.why: It names one action, who would do it and who it is for. The others express a feeling but ask for nothing anyone can do.

modules.t: Building a coalition before you need one
modules.d: Approaching unions and subject associations, what to ask for, and how to agree a send time.

steps.d: Allies need time to agree anything. Approach them weeks before the petition opens, not on the day.
For example: share the link with your members on the first morning. A small, clear ask gets a yes more often than general support.

steps.t: Agree a send time and write it down
steps.d: Shares that land together in the first hours make a petition look alive. Confirm the date and time in writing.
Tell allies what happened, including the numbers, whether it worked or not. They are more likely to help next time.

q.t: When should an ally agree to share your petition?
q.why: Most signatures come early. Agreeing before launch means the shares land together when they count most.

modules.d: How committees gather evidence, what written evidence is for, and how the Youth Select Committee does it.

steps.d: Select committees are groups of MPs or peers who examine an area of government or national policy. They can be Commons, Lords or joint committees.

Most evidence is sent in writing first. Committees often choose who to hear in person from the written evidence, and nobody has a right to appear: at the Northern Ireland Assembly the guide says so in as many words.

steps.t: There is an Easy Read guide
steps.d: UK Parliament publishes an Easy Read guide to giving evidence, as well as detailed guides for the Commons and the Lords.
The Youth Select Committee takes evidence in public, broadcast on Parliament TV and recorded in Hansard, and the Government responds to its report.

q.t: Can anyone insist on giving evidence in person to a committee?
opts: Yes, if they sent written evidence
No, the committee chooses its witnesses
q.why: The committee decides who to hear. Sending clear written evidence is the usual way to be noticed.
